moduleTitle: Lesson 4 - WinX Engine and UIA Engine
learningObjectives: Explain what the UIA Engine 3.0 is based on and what it can reach.
Explain what the WinX Engine steers and how it differs from UIA.
Choose between UIA and WinX at scan time and know where that choice is made.
Recognise that the engine decision is made per scan and is bound into the resulting Modules.
Distinguish the calculator display wildcard identifier from its explicit result assertion in the original UIA exercise.

elements.description: Windows applications use different control technologies. UIA and WinX are two available engines, alongside technology-specific engines such as DotNet. Evaluate supported controls and identification before selecting an engine for a large automation suite.

UIA Engine 3.0 accesses controls through Microsoft UI Automation. Tricentis recommends it when the corresponding standard engine does not support the controls but their UI Automation interface permits steering; this is not a guarantee that every Windows element is supported.

WinX steers supported PowerBuilder applications and applications using the Windows UI API. Evaluate its control support and setup requirements rather than treating it as a universal alternative for any UIA identification failure.

elements.text: UIA depends on the application’s UI Automation exposure. WinX documentation describes Windows UI API and PowerBuilder support. Engine choice, control exposure and supported operations all matter.

bulletPoints: UIA = Microsoft UI Automation; recommended when the corresponding standard engine lacks support and UIA can steer the control.
WinX supports Windows UI API and PowerBuilder controls; verify prerequisites.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: Making the choice at scan time

elements.description: Open XScan with Modules → Scan → Application, or Scan → Application from a Module folder. In Select Application, right-click the target application and choose UIA or WinX, then scan and save its controls. This creates technology-specific Modules.

A scanned Module contains engine-specific identification and control information. Selecting a different engine for another scan does not automatically convert existing Modules or TestSteps. Evaluate new Modules and affected test references before migrating.

elements.text: Tricentis does give UIA selection guidance: use it for controls unsupported by their corresponding standard engine when UI Automation can steer them. For WinX, inspect Windows UI API/PowerBuilder support and scan results. Rescanning is an evaluation step, not a promise that the alternative engine will identify every control.

The original theory demonstrates an MFC application scanned with WinX and Calculator scanned with UIA; resulting Module/ModuleAttribute properties show Engine=WinX or Engine=UIA. Its source-era technology examples and control list are not a current compatibility matrix. English subtitles accidentally say Linux Engine in the WinX demonstration; the selected engine and surrounding narration are WinX, not a Linux automation engine.

bulletPoints: Scan → right-click the application tile → UIA or WinX.
Changing scan technology requires evaluating new Modules and their test references; it is not an automatic TestStep conversion.

elements.description: The Module → TestStep → TestStepValue workflow remains familiar. ActionModes and properties still depend on the control and engine; do not assume every control supports Input, Verify, Buffer and Select identically. UIA table cell input uses embedded controls.

elements.text: Check supported controls and prerequisites before escalating to extensions or image recognition. For disappearing context menus, the documented TBox Context Menu workflow can avoid scanning them. PowerBuilder DataWindow recognition requires enabling the application before scanning.

The original four-page UIA exercise has been read and visually inspected; its calculator example is independently summarized below. The complete theory subtitle text was also reviewed, with selected source frames inspected. Original Academy material is not redistributed, and these source checks are not installed execution.

bulletPoints: Familiar TestStep structure does not imply identical control capabilities.
Use the documented control-specific workflow before choosing an extension or visual fallback.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: Original exercise: identify the display, then verify the result

elements.term: Changing display identity versus expected value
elements.description: The original AE1 exercise scans Calculator with UIA and saves One, Plus, Equals and the Generic GUI display. It changes the display Technical Id Name from Display is 0 to Display is *. This permits identifying the display after its name changes during calculation. The saved attribute can still be named Display is 0; renaming that attribute alone is not changing its technical identifier.

items: In the imported training workspace, scan Calculator from AE1 Exercises > Modules > UIA Engine, choosing UIA in XScan. Inspect and save the required controls.
Change the display Technical Id Name to Display is *; verify that this still identifies the intended display uniquely in the actual target.
Create a TestCase under AE1 Exercises > TestCases > UIA Engine. The source repeats the Calculator Module for One, Plus, One and Equals, each with Value X and ActionMode Input.
Add a separate display assertion: Value .Name==Display is 2 with ActionMode Verify. The wildcard identifier finds the control; this assertion checks the expected name/result.
Run in ScratchBook and inspect the actual result. WorkState Completed is a design status; setting it does not demonstrate successful execution.

elements.text: These names and values belong to the original Tosca 16.0 course/Calculator example. Current Calculator versions, UI language, mode, initial state and UI Automation exposure can differ. Confirm the actual property/value and clear starting state before expecting 1 + 1 = 2. The source expected outcome is not a fresh test result here.

examPitfalls.title: Looking for an engine setting on the Module or TestStep
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Trying to switch a Windows Module from UIA to WinX by editing a property after the scan.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Select the engine in XScan and evaluate the resulting Modules. Changing the scan technology does not automatically convert existing test references; validate any migration.

examPitfalls.title: Confusing which engine uses Microsoft's UI Automation framework
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Attributing the Microsoft UI Automation basis to WinX.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: UIA uses Microsoft UI Automation. WinX is documented for Windows UI API and PowerBuilder applications; keep those support descriptions separate.

examPitfalls.title: Assuming one engine is universally better
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Standardising on UIA (or WinX) for every Windows application on principle.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Start from technology and control support. UIA is recommended where the corresponding standard engine lacks support but UI Automation can steer the controls; validate an alternative scan before migrating tests.

examPitfalls.title: Assuming every ActionMode works on every scanned control
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Treating the common TestStep workflow as proof of identical Input, Verify, Buffer and Select support.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Consult the control-specific steering reference. For UIA table cell entry, use the embedded TextBox, ComboBox or CheckBox control as appropriate.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which framework is the UIA Engine 3.0 based on?

options.text: The Windows UI API, accessed directly.
The Microsoft UI Automation framework.
The Java Access Bridge.
The XBrowser DOM interface.

practiceQuiz.hint: The engine's name is an abbreviation of the framework it uses.
practiceQuiz.rationale: UIA accesses the target through Microsoft UI Automation. Success depends on what that interface exposes; it is not a universal Windows-control guarantee.

optionExplanations.A: This does not name UIA’s documented Microsoft UI Automation interface.
optionExplanations.B: This is the framework on which UIA Engine 3.0 is based.
optionExplanations.C: Java Access Bridge concerns Java accessibility, not UIA’s Microsoft interface.
optionExplanations.D: DOM-based browser identification is not the UIA engine’s basis.

practiceQuiz.scenario: At what point do you choose between UIA and WinX for a Windows desktop application?

options.text: In the TestStep's ActionMode dropdown.
In the project's Engine settings, applied globally.
During scanning — right-click the application's tile and select UIA or WinX from the context menu.
Tosca decides automatically and the choice cannot be influenced.

practiceQuiz.hint: The decision is made at the moment the Modules are created.
practiceQuiz.rationale: After selecting the desktop application to scan, you right-click its tile and choose UIA or WinX. That choice determines whether UIA Modules or Windows UI API Modules are created, and it is bound into those Modules.

optionExplanations.A: ActionMode selects a control operation, not the XScan technology.
optionExplanations.B: The documented choice is made for the application in XScan, not as a universal project setting.
optionExplanations.C: The application selection context menu exposes the scan-engine choice.
optionExplanations.D: The scan workflow permits explicitly selecting UIA or WinX.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A team wants to evaluate WinX for supported controls that were unreliable in its UIA scan. What is an appropriate approach?

options.text: Change a Module property to switch the engine to WinX.
Create a WinX scan and evaluate its Modules and affected test references before migrating.
Abandon desktop automation for that application.
Convert the Modules to XBrowser Modules.

practiceQuiz.hint: Evaluate the supported alternative and its references rather than assuming an automatic conversion.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Creating a scan with the alternative engine permits evaluation of its control identification. The choice does not automatically convert the existing Modules or guarantee success.

optionExplanations.A: Editing a property is not a supported automatic conversion of the scanned identification and test references.
optionExplanations.B: A new scan allows control-support and reference evaluation before migration.
optionExplanations.C: An unreliable scan does not show that all desktop automation is impossible.
optionExplanations.D: Browser Modules do not automatically replace Windows application controls.

practiceQuiz.scenario: When does Tricentis recommend considering UIA Engine 3.0?

options.text: When the corresponding standard engine lacks control support but UI Automation can steer those controls.
Whenever a PDF must be compared, regardless of control technology.
For every Windows application, without checking control support.
Only when a mail server inbox must be read.

practiceQuiz.hint: The recommendation depends on the control’s supported interface.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The UIA engine page explicitly makes this recommendation conditional on standard-engine support and the ability to steer via UI Automation.

optionExplanations.A: This is the conditional recommendation stated on the UIA engine page.
optionExplanations.B: PDF comparison is covered by its dedicated workflow, not this UIA recommendation.
optionExplanations.C: Support must be checked; UIA is not prescribed for every Windows application.
optionExplanations.D: Mailbox access is not the UIA control-steering use case.

practiceQuiz.scenario: How do you scan with the UIA or WinX engines when using the TBox framework in Tosca?

options.text: By launching the XScan, right clicking on the thumbnail of the page to scan, and selecting 'UIA' or 'WinX' from the dropdown list.
By selecting 'Scan Application' and choosing either UIA or WinX from the list.
By right clicking on a Module, selecting 'Rescan', and selecting WinX or UIA from the XScan window.
By launching the XScan from the 'Tools' ribbon and choosing either UIA or WinX.

practiceQuiz.hint: The choice is made on the scanned application's own tile, inside the XScan window.
practiceQuiz.rationale: In the XScan, you right-click the thumbnail of the application/page to scan and pick 'UIA' or 'WinX' from the list that appears. This is the same scan-time decision covered earlier in the lesson — the engine is bound into the Modules the scan produces, so it has to be chosen here, not afterwards.

optionExplanations.A: XScan’s application context menu provides this explicit technology choice.
optionExplanations.B: This omits the application-specific context-menu choice inside XScan.
optionExplanations.C: A rescan does not establish automatic technology conversion of existing Modules and references.
optionExplanations.D: The documented starting route is Scan → Application from Modules or a Module folder.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which types of applications would you scan using the WinX Engine of Tosca?

options.text: Applications that utilize the Windows non UI API.
Applications that utilize the Windows UI API.
Applications based on the Microsoft UI Automation framework.
Web based applications.

practiceQuiz.hint: WinX documentation identifies Windows UI API and PowerBuilder support.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Windows UI API is the documented WinX application category; PowerBuilder is also supported. UIA’s basis is Microsoft UI Automation, and browser control steering uses the relevant browser engine.

optionExplanations.A: This is not the Windows UI API application category documented for WinX.
optionExplanations.B: Windows UI API applications are a documented WinX target category.
optionExplanations.C: Microsoft UI Automation is UIA’s basis, not WinX’s support description.
optionExplanations.D: Browser applications use browser-specific scanning; this is not the stated WinX target category.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which application interface must expose the controls for UIA steering?

options.text: Applications that utilize the Windows UI API.
Applications that utilize the Windows non UI API.
The Microsoft UI Automation interface.
Web based applications.

practiceQuiz.hint: The engine's name is a direct abbreviation of the framework it's built on.
practiceQuiz.rationale: UIA steers through the Microsoft UI Automation interface in the target. The whole application need not be implemented in one particular framework; its controls must expose that interface.

optionExplanations.A: This describes the WinX support category rather than UIA’s required interface.
optionExplanations.B: This is not the UI Automation interface used to steer the controls.
optionExplanations.C: UIA accesses controls through the Microsoft UI Automation interface exposed by the target.
optionExplanations.D: A browser label alone does not establish UIA exposure; browser control testing has its own engine.

quickRecap.value: Microsoft UI Automation interface; conditional on control exposure and support.
Windows UI API and PowerBuilder applications; check supported controls and prerequisites.
At scan time: right-click the application's tile → UIA or WinX.
New scan technology does not automatically convert existing Modules and test references.
UIA has conditional selection guidance; validate technology/control support and scan results.
Familiar TestStep structure; supported ActionModes and properties remain control-specific.
